 I.       The historically and culturally significant Taylor-Rose Ranch is bisected by Link
         G6, which passes a mere 375 feet from the Roses’s home.

         Austin C. and Janet L. Rose are ranchers in Burnet County, living on a historically

and culturally significant ranch that has been in the Taylor family for six generations (the

“Taylor-Rose Ranch”). Janet Rose’s family’s roots run deep in Texas history: her great-

great-great-grandfather William Stanhope Taylor fought with Sam Houston, including at the

Battle of San Jacinto. Later, in 1886, two of William Stanhope Taylor’s sons moved to

Burnet County, buying the ranch land that six generations of Taylors have lived and ranched

on. The Roses live in a home constructed in 1904 and another of the six structures on the

property is an 1886 barn.1

         The Texas Historical Commission (“THC”) has included the entire Taylor-Rose

Ranch in its database of archeologically and culturally significant properties, assigning it

Trinomial No. 41BT562.2 Despite this, twenty-seven of the routes proposed by Oncor

Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation

(“Applicants”)—those that include Link G6—not only bisect the historic working ranch but

also come within 375 feet of the Roses’s home.

         when preparing and updating their Application.

 IV.    Link G6 violates the standards of PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 Tex. Admin. Code

       As discussed in detail below, the use of Link G6, especially as it bisects the

historically and culturally important Taylor-Rose Ranch, violates the statutory

considerations that the Texas Legislature has directed that the Public Utility Commission

consider, PURA § 37.056(c)(4), and also violates the PUC’s own rules, 16 Tex. Admin. Code

§ 25.101(b)(3)(B).

       • Link G6 violates community values, which, in this part of Texas, includes the

           ranching tradition (§37.056(c)(4)(A)).

           Ranch (§37.056(c)(4)(C)).

         B.        The Taylor-Rose Ranch is both historically and culturally significant
                   (§37.056(b)(4)(C)).

         As discussed above, the Taylor-Rose Ranch is a portion of land that was purchased

in 1886 by Janet Rose’s great-great-grandfather, William Washington Taylor (“W. W.

Taylor”). W. W. Taylor had moved in 1883 to Burnet County, acquiring several thousand

acres over the next 40 years.24 His son, William Washington Taylor, Jr. (“Will”), and his

wife Hattie married in 1900 and moved to this ranch. They built their home in 1904—the

same home in which the Roses now reside.25 Over the decades, generations of Taylors

worked the ranch, while also becoming pillars in their community.

         Ms. Rose testified that generations of Taylors have continued their family’s legacy of

being stewards of their land, serving their community, their Country, and believing in God.26

Many descendants later, the ranch purchased in 1886 is now held in trust by Janet Rose and

         D.       The bisection of the Taylor-Rose Ranch, and the placement of the 765-kV
                  line will harm the ranch’s environmental integrity (§37.056(c)(4)(D)).

                  1.        Link G6 would adversely affect the wide diversity of fish, flora and
                            fauna—including some protected species—that live on or frequent
                            the Ranch.

         Ms. Rose testified that hunted species on the Ranch include white-tail deer, wild hogs,

dove, quail, turkey, and squirrel.36 Other species that live on the Ranch (to maintain an

ecological balance) include bobcats, coyotes, red and brown fox, raccoons, opossums,

armadillos, and porcupines.37 Blue heron and egrets eat fish in the water tanks. Birds of

prey, including buzzards, crested caracara, red-tail hawks, and owls, roost on the Ranch.

Bald eagles and golden eagles—both of which are protected under federal law—frequent the

Ranch.38 Crappie, perch, largemouth bass and catfish live in the ponds.39 An alligator

snapping turtle emerges each year, lumbering across the pasture to a stock tank. These

animals, fish, fowl, and reptiles swim or drink from streams, tanks, and water troughs on the

Ranch and forage through and eat from the rich vegetation growing there.40 The 765-kV line

cutting through the ranch—with its destruction of habitat and loud noise—would disturb

those creatures.

birds’ flight patterns. The transmission lines themselves kill birds, either by collision or

electrocution. Also, honeybees exposed to EMF become disoriented and cannot find their

way back to the hives.41 EMF also reduces the bees’ foraging ability.42 Without natural

                 2.       Link G6 would endanger the ranch’s fragile water supply.

        The structures and historic features of the Taylor-Rose Ranch are located on ridges

overlooking several ephemeral tributaries to the Olive Branch stream, which flows northerly

into South Rocky Creek. The Roses have several water wells, which they use for domestic

purposes and to water stock. Burnet County in general, and the northern portion of Burnet

County in particular, lacks sufficient water as it is. The construction of the towers for the

proposed line could very likely exacerbate that.44
